They were three young men, or what remained of them, unspeakably crippled by war, still in uniform, but trundled by their nurses in primitive chariots like the prams of deprived children. Immediately behind them came a large contingent of more grands mutilés. Officers and men of all ranks mixed together, many already in mufti, they marched – or hobbled – without precedence or any semblance of military order, twelve abreast. Hardly one had not lost an eye or a limb, and many bore on their chests France’s most coveted decoration, the Médaille Militaire. The totally blind – some accorded the privilege of being ensign-bearers – came led by the one-legged, or the armless; men with their destroyed faces mercifully hidden behind bandages; men with no hands; men with their complexions still tinted green from the effects of chlorine; men with mad eyes staring out from beneath the skull caps which concealed some appalling head injury. Some were famous heroes, easily recognized by the crowd; among them, identifiable by his immense stature, limped Sergeant André Maginot, already a well-known figure in the Assembly, badly wounded at Verdun.

ELI5 how messages from our deep space probes, like New Horizons, are able to transmit data billions of miles without lost / corrupted data?

Hi, hardware engineer here.

When you design your transmitter/receiver pair, you have to factor in your expected amount of noise. In sound equipment (think speakers, high end headphones) you'll often find a specification for the SNR (signal-to-noise ratio), which is measured in dB. For sound equipment, a higher SNR is better since it means you get less electrical noise in your music. For receivers, you'll have an SNR tolerance. If there's more noise than that SNR tolerance, you're likely to get errors in transmission. But below that tolerance, you've built the receiver in such a way that you've probabilistically modeled the expected noise, and can correct the incoming transmission to what would be more likely to receive when you notice small errors due to noise.

So if you know your probe is going to be really far away, the signal will likely be very weak. Thus you design your receiver with a large signal to noise tolerance for the type of noise you expect to receive. You can characterize the expected noise by taking recordings of the sky in the frequency band you're looking to transmit on. When I was learning the math for this back in school, we would usually be lazy and assume the noise would be Gaussian, since for electrical noise it's not a bad assumption. Unfortunately I don't remember enough to give you equations, but I hope this helps
